recipes.title: Absolute extrema on a closed interval
recipes.type: Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $f(x)=\text{Expression}(x)$ on the closed interval $[a,b]$.

example.problem: Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $f(x)=x^3-3x+2$ on the interval $[0,2]$.

steps.do: Find the critical numbers of $f(x)$ by solving $f'(x)=0$ (and where $f'$ is undefined).
steps.work: $f'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1)$. Solving $3(x-1)(x+1)=0$ gives the critical numbers $x=-1$ and $x=1$.

steps.do: The slate of finalists: the critical numbers from step 1 that lie in the interval, plus the endpoints $a$ and $b$.
steps.work: $x=-1$ is not in $[0,2]$ but $x=1$ is. The finalists are $\{0,\,1,\,2\}$.

steps.do: Plug each finalist into $f(x)$ and compare. The smallest score is the absolute minimum value, the largest is the absolute maximum value.

example.answer: Absolute minimum value $0$ (at $x=1$); absolute maximum value $4$ (at $x=2$).

recipes.topic: The Mean Value Theorem and Monotonicity
recipes.title: Mean Value Theorem: finding c
recipes.type: Verify that $f(x)=\text{Expression}(x)$ satisfies the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem on the interval $[a,b]$. Then find all numbers $c$ that satisfy the conclusion of the Mean Value Theorem.

example.problem: Verify that $f(x)=x^3+x-1$ satisfies the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem on $[0,2]$. Then find all numbers $c$ that satisfy its conclusion.

steps.do: Verify that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Polynomials, exponentials, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ always are. Watch out for denominators that vanish and for radicals.
steps.work: $f(x)=x^3+x-1$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable everywhere. The MVT applies.

steps.do: Find $f'(x)$ and set up the equation $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, where $c$ is still a symbol.
Solve the equation of step 2 for $c$, and keep the solution(s) that lie in the open interval $(a,b)$.
steps.work: $3c^2+1=5$ means $c^2=\tfrac43$, so $c=\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}=\pm\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{3}$. The negative root is not in $(0,2)$; the positive one is.

practice.problem: Verify that $f(x)=x^3-2x$ satisfies the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem on $[0,3]$. Then find the number $c$ in $(0,3)$ that satisfies its conclusion. Enter $c$.

steps.do: Find $f'(x)$ and set up the equation $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, where $c$ is still a symbol.
Solve the equation of step 2 for $c$, and keep the solution(s) that lie in the open interval $(a,b)$.

practice.problem: Verify that $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ satisfies the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem on $[1,9]$. Then find the number $c$ in $(1,9)$ that satisfies its conclusion. Enter $c$.

steps.do: Verify that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Polynomials, exponentials, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ always are. Watch out for denominators that vanish and for radicals.
steps.work: $\sqrt{x}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, which contains $[1,9]$, and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, which contains $(1,9)$. The MVT applies.

steps.do: Find $f'(x)$ and set up the equation $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, where $c$ is still a symbol.
Solve the equation of step 2 for $c$, and keep the solution(s) that lie in the open interval $(a,b)$.
steps.work: $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt c}=\dfrac14$ means $\sqrt c=2$, so $c=4$, which lies in $(1,9)$.

recipes.topic: The Mean Value Theorem and Monotonicity
recipes.title: Showing exactly one root
recipes.type: Show that the equation $f(x)=0$, with $f(x)=\text{Polynomial}(x)$ of odd degree, has exactly one real root.

example.problem: Show that the equation $f(x)=1+5x+4x^3+11x^5+9x^7=0$ has exactly one real root.

steps.do: Check that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$ are $-\infty$ and $\infty$ (or the other way around). By the Intermediate Value Theorem $f$ crosses the $x$-axis, so $f(x)=0$ has at least one root. (This always happens for odd degree.)
steps.work: $f$ is a polynomial of odd degree $7$ with positive leading coefficient, so $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=-\infty$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=\infty$. Hence $f(x)=0$ has at least one real root.

steps.do: Find $f'(x)$ and show it is always positive (or always negative), e.g. all its terms have even degree and positive coefficients.
Conclude by Rolle's Theorem that there cannot be two roots. Together with step 1, there is exactly one root.
steps.work: Suppose there were two real roots $x=a$ and $x=b$ with $f(a)=f(b)=0$. By Rolle's Theorem there would be a $c$ in $(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=0$. But $f'$ is always positive: a contradiction. So there is at most one root, and by step 1 exactly one.

practice.problem: Show that $x^5+3x^3+2x-10=0$ has exactly one real root. Enter whether $f'(x)$ is positive or negative for all $x$.

steps.do: Check that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$ are $-\infty$ and $\infty$ (or the other way around). By the Intermediate Value Theorem $f$ crosses the $x$-axis, so $f(x)=0$ has at least one root. (This always happens for odd degree.)
steps.work: $f(x)=x^5+3x^3+2x-10$ has odd degree $5$ and positive leading coefficient, so $f\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $f\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. At least one real root.

steps.do: Find $f'(x)$ and show it is always positive (or always negative), e.g. all its terms have even degree and positive coefficients.
Conclude by Rolle's Theorem that there cannot be two roots. Together with step 1, there is exactly one root.
steps.work: Two roots $a<b$ would give, by Rolle's Theorem, a $c$ with $f'(c)=0$, impossible since $f'>0$. So at most one root, hence exactly one.

practice.answer: Exactly one real root; $f'(x)$ is positive for all $x$.

practice.problem: Show that $3-2x-x^5=0$ has exactly one real root. Enter whether $f'(x)$ is positive or negative for all $x$.

steps.do: Check that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$ are $-\infty$ and $\infty$ (or the other way around). By the Intermediate Value Theorem $f$ crosses the $x$-axis, so $f(x)=0$ has at least one root. (This always happens for odd degree.)
steps.work: $f(x)=3-2x-x^5$ has odd degree $5$ and negative leading coefficient, so $f\to\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $f\to-\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. At least one real root.

steps.do: Find $f'(x)$ and show it is always positive (or always negative), e.g. all its terms have even degree and positive coefficients.
Conclude by Rolle's Theorem that there cannot be two roots. Together with step 1, there is exactly one root.
steps.work: Two roots $a<b$ would give, by Rolle's Theorem, a $c$ with $f'(c)=0$, impossible since $f'<0$. So at most one root, hence exactly one.

practice.answer: Exactly one real root; $f'(x)$ is negative for all $x$.

recipes.topic: The Mean Value Theorem and Monotonicity
recipes.title: Bounding a function with its derivative
recipes.type: If $f(a)=A$ and $f'(x)\ge C$ for $a\le x\le b$, how small can $f(b)$ possibly be?

example.problem: If $f(2)=3$ and $f'(x)\ge4$ for $2\le x\le5$, how small can $f(5)$ possibly be?

steps.do: By the MVT there is a $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=\dfrac{f(b)-A}{b-a}$. We are told $f'(x)\ge C$ for every $x$, in particular at that $c$. So $\dfrac{f(b)-A}{b-a}\ge C$.
steps.work: By the MVT there is a $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(5)-f(2)}{5-2}=\dfrac{f(5)-3}{3}$. Since $f'(x)\ge4$, $$\dfrac{f(5)-3}{3}\ge4$$

steps.do: Solve the inequality of step 1 for $f(b)$.

example.answer: The smallest $f(5)$ can possibly be is $15$.

practice.problem: If $f(1)=-2$ and $f'(x)\ge5$ for $1\le x\le4$, how small can $f(4)$ possibly be? Enter the smallest possible value.

steps.do: By the MVT there is a $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=\dfrac{f(b)-A}{b-a}$. We are told $f'(x)\ge C$ for every $x$, in particular at that $c$. So $\dfrac{f(b)-A}{b-a}\ge C$.
steps.work: By the MVT there is a $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}=\dfrac{f(4)+2}{3}$. Since $f'(x)\ge5$, $$\dfrac{f(4)+2}{3}\ge5$$

steps.do: Solve the inequality of step 1 for $f(b)$.

practice.answer: The smallest $f(4)$ can possibly be is $13$.

practice.problem: If $f(0)=7$ and $f'(x)\ge-2$ for $0\le x\le3$, how small can $f(3)$ possibly be? Enter the smallest possible value.

steps.do: By the MVT there is a $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=\dfrac{f(b)-A}{b-a}$. We are told $f'(x)\ge C$ for every $x$, in particular at that $c$. So $\dfrac{f(b)-A}{b-a}\ge C$.
steps.work: By the MVT there is a $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(3)-f(0)}{3-0}=\dfrac{f(3)-7}{3}$. Since $f'(x)\ge-2$, $$\dfrac{f(3)-7}{3}\ge-2$$

steps.do: Solve the inequality of step 1 for $f(b)$.

practice.answer: The smallest $f(3)$ can possibly be is $1$.

recipes.title: Increasing, extrema and concavity of a polynomial
recipes.type: Given a function $f(x)=\text{Polynomial}(x)$: (a) find the intervals on which $f$ is increasing or decreasing; (b) find the local maximum and minimum values of $f$; (c) find the intervals of concavity and the inflection points.

steps.do: (a) Find $f'(x)$ and the critical numbers (solve $f'(x)=0$, and add any ‘blow-up’ points). They cut the real line into intervals. Test the sign of $f'$ at a convenient point in each interval: positive means $f$ is increasing, negative means decreasing.
steps.work: $f'(x)=-6x+3x^2=3x(x-2)$, so the critical numbers are $x=0$ and $x=2$. Test points: $f'(-1)=9>0$, so $f$ is increasing on $(-\infty,0)$; $f'(1)=-3<0$, so $f$ is decreasing on $(0,2)$; $f'(3)=9>0$, so $f$ is increasing on $(2,\infty)$.

steps.do: (b) At each critical number compare the interval on its left with the one on its right: increasing then decreasing is a local maximum, decreasing then increasing is a local minimum, no change is neither. Plug the critical number into $f$ for the local value.
steps.work: At $x=0$ the function goes from increasing to decreasing: a local maximum, with value $f(0)=5$ (a peak at $(0,5)$). At $x=2$ it goes from decreasing to increasing: a local minimum, with value $f(2)=5-12+8=1$ (a valley at $(2,1)$).

steps.do: (c) Find $f''(x)$ and solve $f''(x)=0$ (add ‘blow-up’ points). Test the sign of $f''$ in each interval: positive means concave up, negative means concave down. A change of concavity is an inflection point.
steps.work: $f''(x)=6x-6=0$ gives $x=1$. $f''(0)=-6<0$: concave down on $(-\infty,1)$. $f''(2)=6>0$: concave up on $(1,\infty)$. The inflection point is at $x=1$, with $f(1)=5-3+1=3$: the point $(1,3)$.

example.answer: Increasing on $(-\infty,0)$ and $(2,\infty)$, decreasing on $(0,2)$. Local maximum at $(0,5)$, local minimum at $(2,1)$. Concave down on $(-\infty,1)$, concave up on $(1,\infty)$. Inflection point $(1,3)$.

practice.problem: Do (a), (b), (c) for $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$. Enter the local maximum value.

steps.do: (a) Find $f'(x)$ and the critical numbers (solve $f'(x)=0$, and add any ‘blow-up’ points). They cut the real line into intervals. Test the sign of $f'$ at a convenient point in each interval: positive means $f$ is increasing, negative means decreasing.
steps.work: $f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)$, so the critical numbers are $x=1$ and $x=3$. $f'(0)=9>0$: increasing on $(-\infty,1)$. $f'(2)=-3<0$: decreasing on $(1,3)$. $f'(4)=9>0$: increasing on $(3,\infty)$.

steps.do: (b) At each critical number compare the interval on its left with the one on its right: increasing then decreasing is a local maximum, decreasing then increasing is a local minimum, no change is neither. Plug the critical number into $f$ for the local value.
steps.work: $x=1$ goes from increasing to decreasing: a local maximum, value $f(1)=1-6+9+1=5$. $x=3$ goes from decreasing to increasing: a local minimum, value $f(3)=27-54+27+1=1$.

steps.do: (c) Find $f''(x)$ and solve $f''(x)=0$ (add ‘blow-up’ points). Test the sign of $f''$ in each interval: positive means concave up, negative means concave down. A change of concavity is an inflection point.
steps.work: $f''(x)=6x-12=0$ gives $x=2$. $f''(0)=-12<0$: concave down on $(-\infty,2)$. $f''(3)=6>0$: concave up on $(2,\infty)$. The inflection point is $(2,\,f(2))=(2,3)$.

practice.answer: Local maximum value $5$ at $(1,5)$; local minimum value $1$ at $(3,1)$; inflection point $(2,3)$.

practice.problem: Do (a), (b), (c) for $f(x)=2x^3+3x^2-12x$. Enter the inflection point as $(x,y)$.

steps.do: (a) Find $f'(x)$ and the critical numbers (solve $f'(x)=0$, and add any ‘blow-up’ points). They cut the real line into intervals. Test the sign of $f'$ at a convenient point in each interval: positive means $f$ is increasing, negative means decreasing.
steps.work: $f'(x)=6x^2+6x-12=6(x+2)(x-1)$, so the critical numbers are $x=-2$ and $x=1$. $f'(-3)=24>0$: increasing on $(-\infty,-2)$. $f'(0)=-12<0$: decreasing on $(-2,1)$. $f'(2)=24>0$: increasing on $(1,\infty)$.

steps.do: (b) At each critical number compare the interval on its left with the one on its right: increasing then decreasing is a local maximum, decreasing then increasing is a local minimum, no change is neither. Plug the critical number into $f$ for the local value.
steps.work: $x=-2$ is a local maximum, value $f(-2)=-16+12+24=20$. $x=1$ is a local minimum, value $f(1)=2+3-12=-7$.

steps.do: (c) Find $f''(x)$ and solve $f''(x)=0$ (add ‘blow-up’ points). Test the sign of $f''$ in each interval: positive means concave up, negative means concave down. A change of concavity is an inflection point.
steps.work: $f''(x)=12x+6=0$ gives $x=-\tfrac12$. $f''(-1)=-6<0$: concave down on $(-\infty,-\tfrac12)$. $f''(0)=6>0$: concave up on $(-\tfrac12,\infty)$. $f(-\tfrac12)=-\tfrac14+\tfrac34+6=\tfrac{13}{2}$, so the inflection point is $\left(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{13}{2}\right)$.

practice.answer: Local maximum value $20$ at $(-2,20)$; local minimum value $-7$ at $(1,-7)$; inflection point $\left(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{13}{2}\right)$.

recipes.title: Second Derivative Test
recipes.type: Find the critical points of $f(x)$ and use the Second Derivative Test (if possible) to determine whether each corresponds to a local minimum or maximum.

example.problem: Find the critical points of $f(x)=3x^5-5x^3$ and use the Second Derivative Test (if possible) to decide whether each is a local minimum or maximum.

steps.do: Compute $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$.
Find the critical points by solving $f'(x)=0$.
Plug each critical point into $f''(x)$: positive means a local minimum, negative means a local maximum, zero means we don't know (the test is inconclusive).
steps.work: $f''(-1)=-60+30=-30<0$, so $x=-1$ is a local maximum. $f''(0)=0$, so for $x=0$ we don't know. $f''(1)=60-30=30>0$, so $x=1$ is a local minimum. (By the First Derivative Test, $f'$ does not change sign at $x=0$, so it is neither: a horizontal inflection point.)

example.answer: Local maximum at $x=-1$, local minimum at $x=1$, and the test is inconclusive at $x=0$ (it is neither).

practice.problem: Find the critical points of $f(x)=x^4-4x^3$ and use the Second Derivative Test (if possible). Enter the $x$-value of the local minimum.

steps.do: Compute $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$.
Find the critical points by solving $f'(x)=0$.
Plug each critical point into $f''(x)$: positive means a local minimum, negative means a local maximum, zero means we don't know (the test is inconclusive).
steps.work: $f''(0)=0$, so for $x=0$ we don't know. (Since $f'(x)=4x^2(x-3)$ is negative on both sides of $0$, it is neither a max nor a min.) $f''(3)=108-72=36>0$, so $x=3$ is a local minimum.

practice.answer: Local minimum at $x=3$; the test is inconclusive at $x=0$.

practice.problem: Find the critical points of $f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x$ and use the Second Derivative Test. Enter the $x$-value of the local maximum.

steps.do: Compute $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$.
Find the critical points by solving $f'(x)=0$.
Plug each critical point into $f''(x)$: positive means a local minimum, negative means a local maximum, zero means we don't know (the test is inconclusive).
steps.work: $f''(1)=-6<0$, so $x=1$ is a local maximum. $f''(2)=6>0$, so $x=2$ is a local minimum.

practice.answer: Local maximum at $x=1$, local minimum at $x=2$.

recipes.title: Sketching a polynomial curve
recipes.type: Sketch the curve $y=\text{Polynomial}(x)$.

example.problem: Sketch the curve $y=x^4+4x^3$.

steps.do: Find the first and second derivatives $dy/dx$ and $d^2y/dx^2$.
Find the critical numbers by solving $dy/dx=0$, and the potential inflection points by solving $d^2y/dx^2=0$. Combine them into the important numbers.
steps.work: $4x^2(x+3)=0$ gives $x=-3$ and $x=0$. $12x(x+2)=0$ gives $x=-2$ and $x=0$. Important numbers: $x=-3,\,-2,\,0$.

steps.do: Plug the important numbers into $y$ to get the important points.
Use the second derivative test on the critical numbers: local maximum if $d^2y/dx^2<0$, local minimum if $>0$, and if it is $0$ check whether $dy/dx$ changes sign.
steps.work: At $x=-3$: $y''=12(-3)(-1)=36>0$, a local minimum. At $x=0$: $y''=0$, inconclusive; $y'=4x^2(x+3)$ is positive on both sides of $0$, so $x=0$ is neither: a horizontal inflection point.

steps.do: Summarize each important point and its claim to fame.
steps.work: $(-3,-27)$: local minimum. $(-2,-16)$: inflection point. $(0,0)$: horizontal inflection point.

steps.do: Mark the important points on the $xy$-plane (a little cup at a minimum, a cap at a maximum, a short underline at a horizontal inflection point) and connect the dots.
steps.work: Coming from the upper left the curve falls to the valley at $(-3,-27)$ and then rises for good. It is concave up until $(-2,-16)$, concave down between $-2$ and $0$, flattens out at the origin, and then rises concave up to the upper right.

recipes.title: Sketching a rational curve
recipes.type: Sketch the curve $y=\text{Rational}(x)$.

example.problem: Sketch the curve $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2-9}$.

steps.do: Find the horizontal asymptotes by taking the limit as $x\to\infty$ (and $x\to-\infty$). Find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator equal to $0$.
steps.work: Horizontal asymptote: $\displaystyle y=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{x}{x^2-9}=0$. Vertical asymptotes: $x^2-9=0$ gives $x=-3$ and $x=3$.

steps.do: Find $dy/dx$ and $d^2y/dx^2$. Find the critical numbers (besides the vertical asymptotes) by solving $dy/dx=0$ and classify them with the second derivative test. Find the inflection points by solving $d^2y/dx^2=0$.
steps.work: $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{x^2+9}{(x^2-9)^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2x(x^2+27)}{(x^2-9)^3}$$ Critical numbers: $dy/dx=0$ would need $x^2+9=0$, which has no real roots, so there is no local maximum or minimum. Inflection point: $x=0$, where $y=0$. So $(0,0)$ is an inflection point, with slope $-\tfrac19$ there.

steps.do: For each vertical asymptote $x=a$ find $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$, each of which is $\infty$ or $-\infty$. The sign of $y$ on each side tells you which.
steps.work: $y=\dfrac{x}{(x-3)(x+3)}$ is negative for $x<-3$, so $\lim_{x\to-3^-}f(x)=-\infty$ (the curve shoots down before $x=-3$). It is positive between $-3$ and $0$, so it comes down from $+\infty$ after $x=-3$. It is negative just before $x=3$, so it shoots down to $-\infty$ at $x=3$, and positive for $x>3$, so it comes down from $+\infty$ after $x=3$.

example.answer: Asymptotes $y=0$, $x=-3$, $x=3$; no extrema; inflection point $(0,0)$ with slope $-\tfrac19$.

practice.problem: Sketch the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x^2-1}$. Enter the value $y$ of the horizontal asymptote.

steps.do: Find the horizontal asymptotes by taking the limit as $x\to\infty$ (and $x\to-\infty$). Find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator equal to $0$.
steps.work: Horizontal asymptote: $\displaystyle y=\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\dfrac{x^2}{x^2-1}=1$. Vertical asymptotes: $x^2-1=0$ gives $x=-1$ and $x=1$.

steps.do: Find $dy/dx$ and $d^2y/dx^2$. Find the critical numbers (besides the vertical asymptotes) by solving $dy/dx=0$ and classify them with the second derivative test. Find the inflection points by solving $d^2y/dx^2=0$.
steps.work: $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2x}{(x^2-1)^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{6x^2+2}{(x^2-1)^3}$$ Critical number: $x=0$, and $y''(0)=\dfrac{2}{-1}=-2<0$, so $(0,0)$ is a local maximum. Inflection points: $6x^2+2=0$ has no real roots, so none.

steps.do: For each vertical asymptote $x=a$ find $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$, each of which is $\infty$ or $-\infty$. The sign of $y$ on each side tells you which.
steps.work: $y$ has the sign of $x^2-1$ (the numerator is $\ge0$). For $x<-1$ it is positive, so $\lim_{x\to-1^-}f=+\infty$. Between $-1$ and $1$ it is negative, so $\lim_{x\to-1^+}f=-\infty$ and $\lim_{x\to1^-}f=-\infty$. For $x>1$ it is positive, so $\lim_{x\to1^+}f=+\infty$.

practice.answer: Horizontal asymptote $y=1$; vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$; local maximum $(0,0)$; no inflection points.

practice.problem: Sketch the curve $y=\dfrac{3x}{x^2-1}$. Enter the slope of the curve at its inflection point.

steps.do: Find the horizontal asymptotes by taking the limit as $x\to\infty$ (and $x\to-\infty$). Find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator equal to $0$.

Find $dy/dx$ and $d^2y/dx^2$. Find the critical numbers (besides the vertical asymptotes) by solving $dy/dx=0$ and classify them with the second derivative test. Find the inflection points by solving $d^2y/dx^2=0$.
steps.work: $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{3(x^2+1)}{(x^2-1)^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{6x(x^2+3)}{(x^2-1)^3}$$ Critical numbers: $x^2+1=0$ has no real roots, so no local extrema. Inflection point: $x=0$, where $y=0$. The slope there is $y'(0)=-\dfrac{3\cdot1}{1}=-3$.

steps.do: For each vertical asymptote $x=a$ find $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$, each of which is $\infty$ or $-\infty$. The sign of $y$ on each side tells you which.
steps.work: $y=\dfrac{3x}{(x-1)(x+1)}$. For $x<-1$ it is negative: $\lim_{x\to-1^-}f=-\infty$. For $-1<x<0$ it is positive: $\lim_{x\to-1^+}f=+\infty$. For $0<x<1$ it is negative: $\lim_{x\to1^-}f=-\infty$. For $x>1$ it is positive: $\lim_{x\to1^+}f=+\infty$.

practice.answer: Inflection point $(0,0)$ with slope $-3$; no extrema; asymptotes $y=0$, $x=\pm1$.

recipes.title: Fencing a divided rectangle
recipes.type: A farmer wants to fence an area of $A$ square units and then divide it into $n+1$ parts by placing $n$ fences parallel to one of the sides of the rectangle. What dimensions minimize the cost of the fence?

example.problem: A farmer wants to fence an area of $5000$ square feet and then divide it into $3$ parts by placing $2$ fences parallel to one of the sides of the rectangle. What dimensions minimize the cost of the fence?

steps.do: Give names to the variables of the problem.
steps.work: Call the side parallel to the interior fences $x$, and the other side $y$.

steps.do: Write down the constraint and translate it into mathematics: $xy=A$. Express $y$ in terms of $x$.
Find an expression for the goal function. Here the length of fencing is $2x+2y+nx$.
Using step 2, express the goal function in terms of $x$ alone; call it $f(x)$.
Using calculus, minimize $f(x)$: take its derivative and set it equal to zero.

example.answer: The rectangle should be $50\times100$ feet; the total length of fencing is then $400$ feet.

practice.problem: A farmer wants to fence an area of $1000$ square feet and then divide it into $4$ parts by placing $3$ fences parallel to one of the sides of the rectangle. Enter the dimensions $(x,y)$, where $x$ is the side parallel to the interior fences.

steps.do: Give names to the variables of the problem.
steps.work: Call the side parallel to the interior fences $x$, and the other side $y$.

steps.do: Write down the constraint and translate it into mathematics: $xy=A$. Express $y$ in terms of $x$.
Find an expression for the goal function. Here the length of fencing is $2x+2y+nx$.
Using step 2, express the goal function in terms of $x$ alone; call it $f(x)$.
Using calculus, minimize $f(x)$: take its derivative and set it equal to zero.

practice.problem: A farmer wants to fence an area of $1350$ square feet and then divide it into $2$ parts by placing $1$ fence parallel to one of the sides of the rectangle. Enter the minimum total length of fencing.

steps.do: Give names to the variables of the problem.
steps.work: Call the side parallel to the interior fence $x$, and the other side $y$.

steps.do: Write down the constraint and translate it into mathematics: $xy=A$. Express $y$ in terms of $x$.
Find an expression for the goal function. Here the length of fencing is $2x+2y+nx$.
Using step 2, express the goal function in terms of $x$ alone; call it $f(x)$.
Using calculus, minimize $f(x)$: take its derivative and set it equal to zero.
steps.work: $$f'(x)=3-\dfrac{2700}{x^2}=0\ \Rightarrow\ x^2=900\ \Rightarrow\ x=30,\qquad y=\dfrac{1350}{30}=45$$ The minimum length is $f(30)=3\cdot30+2\cdot45=180$.

practice.answer: The minimum length of fencing is $180$ feet (dimensions $30\times45$).

recipes.title: Farthest point on an ellipse
recipes.type: Find the points on the ellipse $ax^2+by^2=c$ that are furthest from the point $(p,q)$.

example.problem: Find the points on the ellipse $x^2+4y^2=4$ that are furthest from the point $(0,1)$.

steps.do: Write down the formula for the squared distance from a general point $(x,y)$ to the designated point. This is your goal function.
The constraint is the equation of the ellipse. Take one of the variables (whichever is convenient) as the main variable and eliminate the other.
steps.work: $x^2+4y^2=4$ means $x^2=4-4y^2$. It is more convenient to take $y$ as the main variable (here $-1\le y\le1$): $$f(y)=4-4y^2+y^2-2y+1=5-2y-3y^2$$

steps.do: Find the maximum of the goal as a function of the main variable: take the derivative and set it equal to $0$.
steps.work: $f'(y)=-2-6y=0$ gives $y=-\tfrac13$, and then $x^2=4-\tfrac49=\tfrac{32}{9}$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{4\sqrt2}{3}$. (Check: $f(-\tfrac13)=\tfrac{16}{3}$ beats the endpoints $f(1)=0$ and $f(-1)=4$.)

practice.problem: Find the points on the ellipse $x^2+9y^2=9$ that are furthest from the point $(0,2)$. Enter the $y$-coordinate of the farthest points.

steps.do: Write down the formula for the squared distance from a general point $(x,y)$ to the designated point. This is your goal function.
The constraint is the equation of the ellipse. Take one of the variables (whichever is convenient) as the main variable and eliminate the other.
steps.work: $x^2=9-9y^2$. Take $y$ as the main variable (here $-1\le y\le1$): $$f(y)=9-9y^2+y^2-4y+4=13-4y-8y^2$$

steps.do: Find the maximum of the goal as a function of the main variable: take the derivative and set it equal to $0$.
steps.work: $f'(y)=-4-16y=0$ gives $y=-\tfrac14$, and then $x^2=9-\tfrac{9}{16}=\tfrac{135}{16}$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{3\sqrt{15}}{4}$. (Check: $f(-\tfrac14)=\tfrac{27}{2}$ beats $f(1)=1$ and $f(-1)=9$.)

practice.problem: Find the points on the ellipse $4x^2+y^2=16$ that are furthest from the point $(2,0)$. Enter the $x$-coordinate of the farthest points.

steps.do: Write down the formula for the squared distance from a general point $(x,y)$ to the designated point. This is your goal function.
The constraint is the equation of the ellipse. Take one of the variables (whichever is convenient) as the main variable and eliminate the other.
steps.work: $y^2=16-4x^2$. Take $x$ as the main variable (here $-2\le x\le2$): $$f(x)=x^2-4x+4+16-4x^2=20-4x-3x^2$$

steps.do: Find the maximum of the goal as a function of the main variable: take the derivative and set it equal to $0$.
steps.work: $f'(x)=-4-6x=0$ gives $x=-\tfrac23$, and then $y^2=16-\tfrac{16}{9}=\tfrac{128}{9}$, so $y=\pm\dfrac{8\sqrt2}{3}$. (Check: $f(-\tfrac23)=\tfrac{64}{3}$ beats $f(-2)=16$ and $f(2)=0$.)

recipes.title: Cheapest cylindrical can
recipes.type: A cylindrical can (with or without a top) is made to contain $V$ cm$^3$ of liquid. Find the dimensions that minimize the cost of the metal used to make the can. (Variations: two kinds of metal with different prices per unit area.)

example.problem: A cylindrical can without a top is made to contain $V$ cm$^3$ of liquid. Find the dimensions that minimize the cost of the metal.

steps.do: Decide who the variables are.
steps.work: The variables are the radius $r$ and the height $h$.

steps.do: Write down the constraint and express one variable in terms of the other.
steps.work: The volume is fixed at $V$, and the volume of a cylinder is $\pi r^2h$. Constraint: $\pi r^2h=V$, so $h=\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}$.

steps.do: Your goal is to minimize the amount (or cost) of metal. The area has parts: the bottom (and top, if any) and the side.
steps.work: The bottom has area $\pi r^2$ and the side has area $2\pi rh$ (cut it and roll it flat: a rectangle with sides $2\pi r$ and $h$). Goal: $\pi r^2+2\pi rh$, which in terms of $r$ alone is $$f(r)=\pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}$$

steps.do: Use calculus to minimize the goal function.
steps.work: $f'(r)=2\pi r-\dfrac{2V}{r^2}=0$ when $r^3=\dfrac{V}{\pi}$, so $r=\left(\dfrac V\pi\right)^{1/3}$. Then $h=\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}=\left(\dfrac V\pi\right)^{1/3}$.

example.answer: Both the radius and the height should equal $\left(\dfrac V\pi\right)^{1/3}$.

practice.problem: A cylindrical can with a top and bottom is made to contain $54\pi$ cm$^3$ of liquid. Find the dimensions that minimize the amount of metal. Enter the radius.

steps.do: Decide who the variables are.
steps.work: The variables are the radius $r$ and the height $h$.

steps.do: Write down the constraint and express one variable in terms of the other.
Your goal is to minimize the amount (or cost) of metal. The area has parts: the bottom (and top, if any) and the side.
steps.work: Top and bottom: $2\pi r^2$. Side: $2\pi rh$. Goal: $$f(r)=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\cdot\dfrac{54}{r^2}=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{108\pi}{r}$$

steps.do: Use calculus to minimize the goal function.

practice.answer: Radius $3$ cm and height $6$ cm (the height is twice the radius).

practice.problem: A cylindrical can without a top is made to contain $16\pi$ cm$^3$ of liquid. The metal for the bottom costs twice as much per unit area as the metal for the side. Find the dimensions that minimize the cost. Enter the height.

steps.do: Decide who the variables are.
steps.work: The variables are the radius $r$ and the height $h$.

steps.do: Write down the constraint and express one variable in terms of the other.
Your goal is to minimize the amount (or cost) of metal. The area has parts: the bottom (and top, if any) and the side.
steps.work: Measure cost in units where the side costs $1$ per unit area. Bottom: $2\cdot\pi r^2$. Side: $2\pi rh$. Goal: $$f(r)=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\cdot\dfrac{16}{r^2}=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{32\pi}{r}$$

steps.do: Use calculus to minimize the goal function.

recipes.title: Recognizing indeterminate forms
recipes.type: Given the limits of functions $f(x),g(x),\dots$ at $x=a$, decide whether the limit of their quotient $f/g$, product $fg$, difference $f-g$, or power $f^g$ at the same point is an indeterminate form.

example.problem: Given $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=0$, $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=0$, $\lim_{x\to a}p(x)=\infty$, $\lim_{x\to a}q(x)=\infty$, which of the following are indeterminate forms? (a) $\lim[f/g]$ (b) $\lim[f\,p]$ (c) $\lim[p-q]$ (d) $\lim[f^{\,g}]$

steps.do: (a) For a quotient, the limit is indeterminate whenever plugging in gives $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.
steps.work: $\displaystyle\lim\dfrac{f}{g}=\dfrac00$, so this is an indeterminate form.

steps.do: (b) For a product, the limit is indeterminate whenever plugging in gives $0\cdot\infty$ (or $0\cdot(-\infty)$).
steps.work: $\lim f\cdot\lim p=0\cdot\infty$, so it is indeterminate.

steps.do: (c) For a difference, the limit is indeterminate whenever it is of the type $\infty-\infty$.
(d) For a power, the limit is indeterminate whenever it is of the type $0^0$, $\infty^0$ or $1^\infty$.

practice.problem: Given $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=0$, $\lim g(x)=0$, $\lim p(x)=\infty$, $\lim r(x)=1$, how many of the following are indeterminate forms? (a) $\lim[p/f]$ (b) $\lim[g\,p]$ (c) $\lim[p-r]$ (d) $\lim[r^{\,p}]$

steps.do: (a) For a quotient, the limit is indeterminate whenever plugging in gives $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.
steps.work: $\dfrac{p}{f}\to\dfrac{\infty}{0}$: not of the type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ (the quotient blows up), so it is not indeterminate.

steps.do: (b) For a product, the limit is indeterminate whenever plugging in gives $0\cdot\infty$ (or $0\cdot(-\infty)$).
(c) For a difference, the limit is indeterminate whenever it is of the type $\infty-\infty$.
steps.work: $p-r\to\infty-1=\infty$: not of the type $\infty-\infty$, so not indeterminate.

steps.do: (d) For a power, the limit is indeterminate whenever it is of the type $0^0$, $\infty^0$ or $1^\infty$.

practice.problem: Given $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=0$, $\lim p(x)=\infty$, $\lim q(x)=\infty$, $\lim s(x)=2$, how many of the following are indeterminate forms? (a) $\lim[p/q]$ (b) $\lim[f\,p]$ (c) $\lim[p-s]$ (d) $\lim[p^{\,f}]$

steps.do: (a) For a quotient, the limit is indeterminate whenever plugging in gives $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.
(b) For a product, the limit is indeterminate whenever plugging in gives $0\cdot\infty$ (or $0\cdot(-\infty)$).
(c) For a difference, the limit is indeterminate whenever it is of the type $\infty-\infty$.
steps.work: $p-s\to\infty-2=\infty$: not of the type $\infty-\infty$, so not indeterminate.

steps.do: (d) For a power, the limit is indeterminate whenever it is of the type $0^0$, $\infty^0$ or $1^\infty$.

recipes.title: L’Hôpital's rule
recipes.type: Use L'Hôpital's rule, if appropriate, to evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{TOP(x)}{BOT(x)}$.

example.problem: Use L'Hôpital's rule, if appropriate, to evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\dfrac{x^8-1}{x^3-1}$.

steps.do: Plug $x=a$ into $\dfrac{TOP(x)}{BOT(x)}$. If $\dfrac{TOP(a)}{BOT(a)}$ gives $\dfrac00$ or $\dfrac\infty\infty$, L'Hôpital's rule is applicable.
steps.work: Plugging $x=1$ into $\dfrac{x^8-1}{x^3-1}$ gives $\dfrac00$, so L'Hôpital's rule is applicable.

steps.do: Invoke L'Hôpital's rule: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{TOP(x)}{BOT(x)}=\lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{TOP'(x)}{BOT'(x)}$. If you still get an indeterminate form, keep doing it until you get a doable limit.
Evaluate the limit by simplifying and plugging in.

recipes.title: Repeated L’Hôpital's rule
recipes.type: Same as the previous recipe, but now you have to use L'Hôpital's rule more than once.

example.problem: Use L'Hôpital's rule, if appropriate, to evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}$.

steps.do: Plug $x=a$ into $\dfrac{TOP(x)}{BOT(x)}$. If $\dfrac{TOP(a)}{BOT(a)}$ gives $\dfrac00$ or $\dfrac\infty\infty$, L'Hôpital's rule is applicable.
steps.work: Plugging $x=0$ into $\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}$ gives $\dfrac00$, so L'Hôpital's rule is applicable.

steps.do: Invoke L'Hôpital's rule. If you still get an indeterminate form (this time you do!), keep doing it until you get a doable limit.
steps.work: $$\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin x}{2x}$$ Plugging in $x=0$ still gives $\dfrac00$, so do it again: $$=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\cos x}{2}$$

steps.do: Evaluate the limit by simplifying and plugging in.

practice.problem: Use L'Hôpital's rule to evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{x-\sin x}{x^3}$.

steps.do: Plug $x=a$ into $\dfrac{TOP(x)}{BOT(x)}$. If $\dfrac{TOP(a)}{BOT(a)}$ gives $\dfrac00$ or $\dfrac\infty\infty$, L'Hôpital's rule is applicable.
steps.work: Plugging $x=0$ into $\dfrac{x-\sin x}{x^3}$ gives $\dfrac00$, so L'Hôpital's rule is applicable.

steps.do: Invoke L'Hôpital's rule. If you still get an indeterminate form (this time you do!), keep doing it until you get a doable limit.
steps.work: $$\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{x-\sin x}{x^3}=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{3x^2}\ \ (\tfrac00\text{ again})=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin x}{6x}\ \ (\tfrac00\text{ again})=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\cos x}{6}$$

steps.do: Evaluate the limit by simplifying and plugging in.

example.problem: Find the most general antiderivative of $f(x)=5e^x+8\sec^2x$.

steps.do: Memorize the differentiation table in reverse: an antiderivative of $x^n$ is $\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$ (except when $n=-1$), of $\cos x$ is $\sin x$, of $\sin x$ is $-\cos x$, of $\sec^2x$ is $\tan x$, and so on. Do it piece by piece.
steps.work: An antiderivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$, and of $\sec^2x$ is $\tan x$. Hence an antiderivative of $f$ is $5e^x+8\tan x$.

practice.problem: Find the most general antiderivative of $f(x)=4x^3+2\sin x-\dfrac{7}{x^2}$. Enter an antiderivative.

steps.work: $4x^3\to x^4$. $\ 2\sin x\to-2\cos x$. $\ -7x^{-2}\to-7\cdot\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1}=\dfrac7x$. So an antiderivative is $x^4-2\cos x+\dfrac7x$.

recipes.title: Integrating an odd function over a symmetric interval
recipes.type: Use graphical considerations to compute $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}\text{Complicated}(x)\,dx$, where $\text{Complicated}(x)$ happens to be an odd function (recall that $f$ is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$).

example.problem: Use graphical considerations to compute $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\left(\tan(x^3)+3x\right)dx$.

steps.do: The limits of integration must have the form $\int_{-a}^{a}$ (for $\int_{-1}^{2}$ this method fails). Also check that the integrand is odd, by plugging in $-x$ and simplifying: $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
steps.work: The limits have the form $-a$ to $a$ with $a=2$. For $f(x)=\tan(x^3)+3x$: $$f(-x)=\tan\!\left((-x)^3\right)+3(-x)=\tan(-x^3)-3x=-\tan(x^3)-3x=-f(x)$$ (recall that $\tan$ is odd: $\tan(-w)=-\tan w$).

steps.do: Since the function is odd, the region between $x=-a$ and the $y$-axis is the mirror image, upside down, of the region between the $y$-axis and $x=a$. So the “positive area” equals the “negative area”, and their difference is $0$.
steps.work: The region between $x=-2$ and the $y$-axis is the opposite of the region between the $y$-axis and $x=2$, so positive and negative areas cancel.

steps.work: The argument $s$ is the upper limit, the lower limit is the number $\pi$, and $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ is an expression in the integration variable $x$.

steps.do: To differentiate with respect to the upper limit, just replace the integration variable by the upper-limit variable in the integrand.

recipes.topic: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part II
recipes.title: Variable upper limit with chain rule
recipes.type: Use Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to find the derivative of $h(x)=\displaystyle\int_{\text{Number}}^{g(x)}\text{Expr}(r)\,dr$, where the upper limit is an expression $g(x)$ rather than just $x$. (If the lower limit is the variable one, first flip the integral with a minus sign.)

example.problem: Use Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to find the derivative of $h(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{x^2}\sqrt{1+r^3}\,dr$.

steps.do: Here the upper limit is an expression $g(x)$ in the variable of the function on the left, not just the variable itself. Rewrite the derivative with the chain rule: $h'(x)=\dfrac{dg(x)}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{d}{dg(x)}\!\left(\displaystyle\int_{\text{Number}}^{g(x)}\text{Expr}(r)\,dr\right)$.
Differentiate $g(x)$, and do the other part exactly as in the previous recipe, plugging $g(x)$ in for the integration variable.

recipes.title: Substitution for an indefinite integral
recipes.type: Evaluate the indefinite integral $\displaystyle\int\text{Complicated}(x)\,dx$ using the substitution rule.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int e^x\sqrt{1+e^x}\,dx$.

steps.do: Try to find a good $u$. Usually what is inside parentheses or a root sign is a good bet. (There may be several obvious choices and usually only one works.)
steps.work: $1+e^x$ is inside the square root, so try $u=1+e^x$.

steps.do: Find $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ and, by ‘cross-multiplying’, express $dx$ in terms of $du$.
Translate from the $x$ language to the $u$ language. You should end up with ONLY $u$ (use algebra if some $x$-stuff remains).
Do this far simpler $u$-integral. Finally replace $u$ by the expression in $x$ it stands for, and add $+C$.

recipes.title: Substitution for a definite integral
recipes.type: Evaluate the definite integral $\displaystyle\int_a^b\text{Complicated}(x)\,dx$ using the substitution rule.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt\pi}x\cos(x^2)\,dx$.

steps.do: As before, try to find a good $u$.
steps.work: $x^2$ is inside the cosine, so try $u=x^2$.

steps.do: Find $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ and, by ‘cross-multiplying’, express $dx$ in terms of $du$.
Translate from $x$ to $u$, and also translate the limits of integration by plugging $a$ and $b$ into $u$. You should get a definite integral involving ONLY $u$. Evaluate it.
